question: Which statement best describes Painting order without z-index?
options: Many things create a new stacking context: a positioned element with a z-index other than auto; opacity less than 1; any transform, filter, perspective, clip-path, or mask; will-change of a context-triggering property; isolation: isolate; position: fixed/sticky; and flex/grid children with a z-index. Each new context traps its children's z-index.

When nothing sets z-index, the browser paints in a defined order: background and borders first, then non-positioned blocks, then floats, then inline content, then positioned elements in source order. So a later positioned element naturally sits on top of an earlier one. z-index only enters the picture to override this default.

z-index has no effect on a statically positioned element (the default). It applies to elements with position: relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky — and to flex and grid items even when statically positioned. This is the single most common reason z-index 'does nothing': the element isn't a stacking participant.

A stacking context is a self-contained group of elements that stack together as a unit. z-index values only compete WITHIN the same stacking context. An element with z-index: 1 inside one context can never appear above an element in a sibling context that stacks higher — no matter how large its z-index.

question: Which statement best describes z-index only works on positioned (or flex/grid) items?

Each new context traps its children's z-index.

When a parent creates a stacking context, its children's z-index values become local to that context. A child with z-index: 9999 can still appear behind a sibling of the PARENT that has a higher z-index, because the child is trapped inside the parent's stack level. The fix is usually to raise the parent or restructure the DOM.
